From scores to catches. A probe raises an alarm when a command's score crosses a threshold, and it catches an attack run if it raises an alarm on any of the run's commands.[8] We set each threshold so that 1% of honest commands raise an alarm, and call that share the alarm level. Real runs use a threshold set on real honest runs, and simulated runs use one set on simulated honest runs, as a fully simulated evaluation would.[9] An honest run gives the probes about 65 to 75 commands to score, so 26% to 43% of honest runs still raise at least one alarm, depending on the probe.[10]

Probes caught attacks about equally often in simulation and in reality

Figure 1. Simulated and real catch rates for six probes, compared to the difference between two real runs. Left, % of attack runs caught. Blue is the average of two real runs, and orange is the simulated run. The black tick marks the share of real honest runs that raise an alarm, about what a random probe would catch if it couldn’t tell attack runs from honest ones. It differs by probe because some probes raise more of their alarms in the same runs, so their alarms reach fewer runs. Right, the difference in catch rate: simulated minus real (orange) and real run 2 minus real run 1 (gray), in percentage points, with 95% intervals from resampling main tasks. The top row shows the average of all six probes, and the second row shows the average of the four best probes (AUROC substantially better than the random baseline).

Averaged over the six probes, probes caught 1.0 percentage points fewer attacks in simulated control evals than in real ones (95% interval −3.0 to +1.0; Figure 1, right panel).[11] For reference, the amount caught varied by 0.2 percentage points between the two real evals (since the agent behaves somewhat differently in each eval).[12]

Restricting to the four probes with AUROC substantially better than the random baseline, probes caught 1.3 percentage points fewer attacks in simulated control evals than in real ones (Figure 1, right panel). For reference, the amount caught varied by 0.6 percentage points between the two real evals.[13]

We can’t rule out small effects, since we don’t have data with sufficient statistical power to do so. But these results suggest that, at least for probe experiments, simulated control evals are acceptably realistic.

A probe can still tell the difference between simulated and real environments

Although probes’ attack-detection performance is similar in simulated and real environments, we find that a linear probe can distinguish activations from simulated vs. real environments (“simulation probe”) with AUROC 0.88 when reading tool outputs and 0.72 when reading commands (AUROC ~0.5 for distinguishing activations from real run 1 vs real run 2). This suggests that there are systematic differences between Qwen3.5’s activations in simulated and real environments, which don’t (substantially) affect probes’ performance at detecting attacks (see Appendix D).

Figure 2. ROC curves for linear probes trained to predict (left) whether Qwen3.5 is in a simulated or real environment and (right) whether a run is real run 1 vs real run 2. Probes use as input the activations from layer 48 at the end of each command Qwen3.5 writes (dashed) or immediately after Qwen3.5 reads tool outputs (solid). Curves show ROCs computed on a held-out test set from the cross-fold validation.

We suspect that probes for detecting attacks in our data are insensitive to the systematic differences between simulated and real environments because these systematic differences arise mostly from superficial differences between tool outputs in simulated and real environments. To test this hypothesis, we train variants of the six probes to score Qwen3.5’s tool outputs (instead of commands).

As we might expect, the simulation probe distinguishes simulated from real environments better on tool outputs than on commands  (AUROC 0.88 vs 0.72). But probes for detecting attacks in Qwen3.5’s tool outputs still perform similarly at detecting attacks in simulated vs. real environments (catch rate in simulated runs is 1.3 points lower than in real runs, with two real runs differing by 0.9 points; see Appendix E).[14] This lends credence to our hypothesis that probes for detecting attacks in our data are insensitive to the systematic differences between simulated and real environments because these systematic differences arise mostly from superficial differences between tool outputs in simulated and real environments.

Does the difference between simulated and real activations hurt monitoring?

Not for Qwen3.5 in our environments. The activations of Qwen3.5 differ between simulated and real runs (the simulation probe separates them with AUROC 0.88 on tool output and 0.72 on commands). However, this didn’t appear to affect the performance of our attack probes: the difference in average performance between the simulated and real setting was small and not distinguishable from 0 (on average over the six probes, attack probes performed 1.0 [95% interval: -3.0, 1.0] percentage points worse in simulation, compared with a difference of 0.2 percentage points between the two real runs). In particular, the upper bound of the confidence interval suggests that monitoring in simulation is unlikely to significantly overestimate safety (by more than ~1 percentage point, which is small compared to the performance of our probes).

However, it’s possible that future models will be more aware of being in simulation and that this awareness might have a larger impact on monitoring performance. It could be encoded more strongly in the activations of future models (giving monitoring probes more opportunity to perform differently as a result), and the models may behave differently if they become aware of being in simulation. It would be valuable to understand if probe monitors begin catching more attacks in simulation than in reality when models become aware of being in simulation, particularly for more capable agents.

This work was done over the course of a two-week sprint by Aswin Surya (lead) under the supervision of James Lucassen. This work was done at Redwood Research as part of Redwood Research’s internship program (through MATS 11.0). Code can be found here.

Appendix

Appendix A. Runs, probes and thresholds in detail

Which runs, probes and thresholds go into each number, and could a probe have trained on the tasks it scores?

All comparisons aggregate three attack runs (two real, one simulated) per task, and score them with six probes. Thresholds are set with honest runs from the same setting (real or simulated). No probe ever sees its own main task in training when we score it.

The runs. For each of 1,313 tasks (corresponding to 864 different ‘main tasks’ since some tasks share a main task), we have three attack runs: two where the agent’s commands are executed on a Linux machine (real runs) and one where a language model simulates the responses to all of the agent’s tool uses (simulated run). Of the 1,000 task pairs evaluated in the simulated control evaluations paper, we were able to include 978 of them here; we describe the 22 tasks we could not include, along with 25 other tasks we excluded, in Appendix H.

Figure 3. Illustration of the three attack runs and honest runs we use for each task, and how they’re used to compute the different comparisons we make.

Probes

Except where noted, probes are linear probes, meaning they compute a weighted sum of the model’s activations and output a score, with higher scores indicating more suspicious behavior. For the deception probe we average together six linear probes, one for each layer. We trained two of the six probes we use (details below); the others have been published previously. We summarize these probes in Table 1 in the main text.

On-policy probe

We fit this probe with logistic regression, using layer 48 out of 64. We train separate probes for commands and tool outputs, learning to distinguish Qwen3.5’s attack runs (real run 1) from its honest runs. Overall there is roughly one attack and one honest run per main task, covering approximately 840 main tasks. To avoid scoring any runs with a probe trained on data from the same main task, we divide main tasks into five groups and train five models, leaving out a different group each time. Each probe is thus trained on data from approximately 670 main tasks, and we score each main task with the probe that did not include that main task in training.

Off-policy probe

We fit this probe with L2-regularized logistic regression, again training separate probes for commands and responses. Here we use Qwen3.5’s activations, but on inputs consisting of entire attack (real run 1; 939 total) and honest (990 total) transcripts generated by GPT-5.6-Sol, learning to tell Sol’s attack and honest runs apart. As before, we train five models leaving out a different group of main tasks each time, and score each main task with a model that did not include that main task in training (if none of the five models included that main task in training, we average their predictions). For commands we use the final layer (layer 63); for responses we use two layers per probe, selected using only in-training data (mostly between layers 45 and 49).

Deception probe

We use the publicly available weights for this probe applied to Qwen3.5-27B: the linear probe, applied to layers 19, 27, 35, 43, 51, 58. As with the other published probes, we apply it to the same activation positions we use elsewhere (see “Where the probes read”), and average together the results from the six layers.

Harmfulness direction

This direction is the difference in mean activations between 128 harmful and 128 harmless publicly available prompts, using the last token of the request and layer 34 (i.e. after the model has processed the user’s request, and potentially learned something about whether it will be harmful).

Refusal direction

This direction is likewise the difference in mean activations between the same 128 harmful and 128 harmless prompts, but using the final token of the prompt (i.e. right before generating its response, and potentially having learned something about whether it will refuse to respond) and layer 47.

High-stakes probe

This is a logistic regression probe using layer 43, trained on conversations generated and labelled by GPT-4o.

Where the probes read

Except where noted, for commands we use the activations near the end of the command, before executing it (this is where a monitor would need to make its decision if it wanted the option of blocking the command). At this point the model will have processed all previous responses, so its activations capture information about the entire run so far. Our probes use the final activation in the tool call, omitting tool calls where this corresponds to some boilerplate (e.g. a timeout parameter at the end); this omits around 14% of the tool calls scored by the published probes. The published probes use the activations at the end of the command itself (so, e.g. for a file editing tool, at the end of instructions like “create” but before the model has specified the file contents). File editing tool calls make up around 17% of honest and 21% of attack commands scored by the published probes, in both the real and simulated settings. For responses (Appendix E), we use the mean activation over all “content tokens” (i.e. excluding boilerplate tokens used to format the chat).

From here on, by an action we mean either a command or a response, whichever is being scored by a given probe. We do not smooth probe scores over time (e.g. with an exponential moving average): each action gets its own probe score. For each run we use probe scores for all actions, including at the beginning and end of the run. Except where noted, for our probes we standardise probe scores using the mean and standard deviation of probe scores on honest data (separately for each of real and simulated data, and for our probes, within each cross-validation fold), so scores are reported in standard deviations; the published probes’ scores are in their original units.

Thresholds

We choose different thresholds for real and simulated data, each calibrated so that 1% of actions in honest runs cross the threshold. If any action in an attack run crosses the threshold we consider the run caught, even if this happens after the model has performed the side task. At a 1% action threshold, between 26% and 43% of honest runs contain at least one action that crosses the threshold, depending on probe and setting.

The threshold for real data is likely to be estimated more precisely than for simulated data, since we set it using around two honest runs per main task (1,906 total), compared to around one per main task (868 total) for simulated data. Since both real runs use the same threshold, the difference between real run 2 and real run 1 does not include uncertainty in the threshold; the difference between simulated and real data does include this uncertainty, and as a result the difference between simulated and real data will tend to vary slightly more than the difference between real run 2 and real run 1, making it slightly harder for simulation to look better than reality on this comparison.

The two thresholds are also calibrated on somewhat different distributions of tasks: real honest runs come from three separate batches of tasks, one of which only included tasks from our oldest task distribution, so this task distribution is over-represented in real data. As mentioned, we also standardise our probes’ scores separately on real and simulated data (and within cross-validation folds), using slightly different rescalings in each case which could in principle affect which attacks cross the threshold. Both of these effects could contribute to the difference we see between catch in simulation and reality.

Uncertainty intervals

Except where noted, uncertainty intervals are computed using 10,000 bootstrap samples, resampling tasks (grouping together different tasks with the same ‘main task’) and recalibrating our thresholds each time. They apply to each quantity individually, not simultaneously to all probes. For comparisons between simulated and real data, we always keep the simulated and real runs for a given task together when resampling, so we’re always comparing performance on the same set of tasks.

The on-policy probe catches almost all attacks even in simulation, so there is little room for a shift, but its interval is much smaller than for the other probes and excludes zero (−0.35, 95% interval −1.31 to −0.02). (Recall that when catch rate is close to 100%, even a shift of less than a point corresponds to just a handful of tasks.) We also trained the on-policy probe using only a tenth as many tasks to see if we could get a probe with mid-range performance; surprisingly, it still caught 98.6% of attacks on whole runs (averaged over two real data collection runs).

The probe with the largest apparent drop in performance in simulation is the off-policy probe: it caught 4.9 percentage points fewer attacks in simulation than on real machines (95% confidence interval −10.8 to +1.1), although the two real data collection runs only differed by less than a point. The next largest shifts were both 2.2 points, for the harmfulness direction (which performed worse in simulation) and deception probes (which performed better).

One potential explanation for the off-policy probe’s drop in performance is that it is responding in part to features of the simulation itself. If so, we would expect the probe’s performance to drop most on simulated trajectories that most obviously differ from real trajectories. To investigate this, after noticing the drop in performance, we compared it to the probe described in Appendix D, which predicts whether commands come from simulations or not. We then used its predictions to measure how obvious each simulated trajectory is. We find no evidence that trajectories which look more obviously simulated to this probe suffer a larger drop in catch rate for the off-policy probe (Spearman correlation between obviousness and drop in catch rate: −0.03, 95% confidence interval −0.09 to +0.02, for comparison: −0.02 between the two real data collection runs).

Another factor that could play a role is that thresholds were set differently. We set a separate alarm threshold for each configuration using its own set of honest runs. We also computed how well probes do at detecting simulated attacks when using thresholds calibrated on actual honest commands; using this calibration procedure, the performance degradation of off-policy probes in the simulation setting drops from 4.9 to 0.7 points (95% interval −3.2 to +3.0). Thus, some of the apparent degradation may be attributable to differences in how thresholds were chosen (using simulated versus actual honest commands) and not to probes actually doing a worse job of scoring simulated versus actual attacks.

It’s worth noting that the probe from Appendix D for detecting simulation only has moderate performance, so it’s still possible that there is a weak relationship between how obviously simulated a trajectory is according to this probe and how much the off-policy probe’s performance degrades on that trajectory. However, given that we have six probes and thus some expectation that one will perform noticeably worse than the rest, we suspect that the off-policy probe’s drop in performance is likely just an idiosyncrasy of that particular probe.

Appendix D. Detecting the simulation from activations

We find that Qwen3.5’s activations provide strong evidence for whether it’s interacting with a simulated environment when processing tool outputs, and somewhat weaker evidence when generating commands. Specifically, we train probes to predict whether model activations come from simulated or real environments and find that these probes achieve an AUROC of 0.88 (when scoring model processing of tool outputs) and 0.72 (when scoring model generation of commands) at distinguishing simulated from real attack trajectories (scoring entire runs as opposed to individual model actions). By comparison, analogous probes at distinguishing between our two data collection runs of real trajectories achieve an AUROC of only 0.49 to 0.50, indicating no ability to make such a distinction.

To train these “simulation probes”, we use all 1,309 simulated attack trajectories and 1,311 real attack trajectories (covering 863 main tasks in total) that we collected. We standardize Qwen3.5’s activations from layer 48 and train L2-regularized logistic regression models to predict whether each activation comes from a simulated or real environment. We perform five-fold cross-validation, splitting folds by main task so that no model is ever scored on activations arising from trajectories from main tasks it was trained on, and score each trajectory using the average score assigned to its held-out actions.

Appendix F. Did the agent behave differently in simulation?

One possible explanation for matching catch rates between simulated and real environments is that probes that inspect shell commands succeed in simulation because they mostly catch what the agent does after writing the command, and the agent does about the same things after reading commands in both environments. However, we have not validated this explanation: we have not studied how attacks differ between environments.

We found no indication from other agent behaviors that attacks in simulation are likely to be meaningfully different from attacks on real machines. The fraction of tasks for which we could clearly identify an attack was 95.7% in simulation, 97.0% and 96.3% in the two real runs (simulated minus real run 1, minus 1.2 percentage points; 95% interval minus 2.6 to plus 0.2). This is of similar magnitude to the difference in catch rate between environments, so if tasks with and without attacks are caught at similar rates in both environments, this difference in attack rate could explain some of the difference in catch rate between environments, instead of probes catching different attacks in the two environments.

Of tasks where we could not clearly identify an attack, many (median 192 steps in simulation, 191 in real machines; median for tasks with attacks was 67, 68 to 69 steps) went close to the 200 step limit, and such tasks might be more likely to be caught than others, in which case this effect would bias catch rates in simulation up instead of down.

Number of steps (average 76) and number of commands (shell commands and file editing commands) were similar between environments, as was (to a lesser degree) the number of output tokens.

Appendix G. Do the same tasks get caught?

Another way catch rates could match between simulated and real environments without probes’ performances transferring well is if they catch different attacks at similar rates. To test this, we compared per-task catch between environments.

We can’t directly compare which attacks probes catch in different runs since it’s often unclear how to match up attacks 1:1 across episodes. However, we can measure whether tasks caught in one environment tend to be caught in the other. When a probe catches most attacks, tasks caught by a probe in one environment will often be caught in the other environment even if probes catch completely different attacks, so we use Cohen’s kappa to measure how much more often than chance tasks caught in one environment are also caught in the other.

On average across probes, kappa between catch in real run 1 and the simulated environment (0.19) is similar to kappa between catch in the two real environments (0.16; difference between environments plus 0.03; 95% interval minus 0.05 to plus 0.10). In other words, tasks caught in real run 1 are caught in the simulated environment about as often as they’re caught in real run 2, and only somewhat more often than chance.

This result is driven by the on-policy probe, which catches almost all attacks and so its kappa estimate is determined by a few tasks it fails to catch and has a wide confidence interval. Excluding the on-policy probe (calculated post-hoc after seeing the result above), kappa is 0.20 between the two real environments and 0.17 between real run 1 and the simulated environment (difference between environments minus 0.03; 95% interval minus 0.06 to plus 0.01). We focus on results including all six probes.

We repeated this analysis for the on-policy probe using the maximum anomaly score instead of whether the anomaly score crossed our threshold. Regression of maximum anomaly score in real run 1 onto maximum anomaly score in real run 2 explains only about 21% of the variance in maximum anomaly score, since attacks often look quite different across environments even between real machines. The simulated environment explains slightly less variance (R squared equals 0.15 instead of 0.21; difference minus 0.05 before rounding; 95% interval minus 0.10 to minus 0.01). However, this result is sensitive to which real environment we use as the baseline: since the on-policy probe is trained on attack runs from real run 1, if we instead baseline against real run 2 the difference in R squared is much smaller (minus 0.02; 95% interval minus 0.06 to plus 0.03).

Appendix H. Tasks and runs we left out

Did dropped tasks or excluded runs tilt the comparison?

We don’t know if or how excluding failed honest runs from calculating anomaly score thresholds biased our results.

We ran 1,360 tasks and report results on 1,313 tasks (all tasks where all three attack runs completed and received scores). Reasons for excluding the other 47 tasks (22 of the 1,000 task pairs from the simulated control evaluations paper) are:

  • agent runs that ended with reasoning but no answer (9)
  • simulator output-format errors (9)
  • environment setup failures before the agent made any model call (9)
  • simulated runs that never started because no usable honest reference run existed (9)
  • tasks whose runs could not be built before launch, so no run of any kind started (3)
  • timeouts with no recorded cause (2), and other failures with no recorded cause (2)
  • tasks excluded while preparing the data for the probes, with no scoreable run (2)
  • one malformed tool call
  • one run that hit the two-hour limit without saving its messages.

Of these, simulator output-format errors and tasks with no usable real honest run for the simulator to work from pertain specifically to the simulator.

We additionally excluded at least 39 real honest runs from calculating anomaly score thresholds: 26 on model-registry tasks, 10 on slack-clone tasks and 3 on tiktok tasks. In each of these runs the agent produced reasoning but no answer twice in a row, which real attack runs rarely did (11 of 2,744). We additionally excluded 34 real honest attempts with no usable model call.

  1. ^

    In a control evaluation, we instruct an agent to attack and measure how frequently safeguards detect the attack. Safety is the probability that monitoring detects an attack before it successfully goes undetected. Simulated control evaluations can predict the safety of five transcript-reading monitors (that raise a flag in 5% of benign trials) with an error (root-mean-square error) of only 3.6 percentage points on LinuxArena (compared with 10.1 using a different control evaluation setting, BashArena). Note that for control evaluations, the simulation doesn’t need to successfully deceive the agent, since we instruct the agent to attack regardless.

  2. ^

    For example, Anthropic's August 2026 frontier risk report mentions using such a probe to highlight potentially impactful tool calls for monitoring by transcript-reading monitors, and both OpenAI and Google DeepMind train classifiers on model activations to detect model misuse. Probes are computationally cheap because they leverage activations computed as part of running the model, and a probe for deception is already effective at detecting sabotage by an agent in SHADE-Arena and BashArena.

  3. ^

    Probes are known to become less reliable as context length increases and can even be sensitive to innocuous changes such as typos, so probe scores may vary based on changes to what the agent sees, even if the agent behaves similarly.

  4. ^

    This is the setup used throughout the simulated control evaluations paper. GPT-6-Astra is much more capable than the agent being simulated. The paper’s simulator uses GPT-5.6-Sol as a backup model if GPT-6-Astra refuses a request or otherwise fails to generate a valid response to make a tool call. The version of the code we used additionally falls back to GPT-5.6-Sol if GPT-6-Astra hallucinates an internet connection error, or if a judge model determines that the agent’s last action was to request downloading or executing code from outside the simulated environment. GPT-5.6-Sol contributed to at least one response in around 42% of attack simulations and 6% of benign simulations. We note that having a real benign simulation for each task is an advantage that labs simulating new tasks may not have.

  5. ^

    Some tasks consist of the same main task with different side tasks, and there are 864 unique main tasks among the 1,313 tasks. 978 of the tasks correspond to task pairs from the simulated control evaluations paper (out of 1,000 task pairs total; the remaining 22 task pairs did not work for us, see Appendix H).

  6. ^

    Ideally, a lab would train its probe using examples of its own agent misbehaving in deployment, but such data can only be collected during deployment, meaning some deployment would have to happen before such a probe could be used. Our “on-policy” probe, which we train using examples of our agent attempting to complete the attack task, is thus a best-case scenario for how in-distribution a probe could be. Our “off-policy” probe corresponds to a scenario where a lab trains its probe using examples from a different agent (e.g. reusing training data from a probe-based monitor it developed for a previous agent). The four published probes correspond to probes a lab could use without having any LinuxArena data. We also experimented with using a probe for evaluation awareness, trained using a technique from a published paper. When we informed Qwen3.5 that it was being evaluated, the probe did not fire, so we couldn’t use it to measure evaluation awareness. Qwen3.5 also verbalized suspicion of being evaluated infrequently, not often enough for us to make a comparison between conditions. Still, it’s worth noting that a model can exhibit evaluation awareness without explicitly expressing suspicion. We did not experiment with informing the agent that it should be wary of potentially being in a simulation.

  7. ^

    All six probes are linear probes, except for the deception probe, which averages predictions from six linear probes. We use the qualifier “approximately” because the exact final token is not always the same. For our two trained probes, the final token refers to the last token in the entire tool call. For the four published probes, the final token refers to the last token in the command, which in the case of editing a file does not include tokens corresponding to the edited content (see Appendix A, “Where the probes read”).

  8. ^

    We include all scored attack simulations, even those (a small minority) where the agent did not unambiguously attempt to complete the side task. In 95.7% of attack simulations (97.0% and 96.3% in the two real runs; see Appendix F), the agent unambiguously attempted to complete the side task.

  9. ^

    We exclude benign simulations where the agent failed to run properly (setup failures, format errors, reasoning with no answer, rate limits). In the non-simulated setting, these comprised 3.8% of benign simulations (a lower bound since some earlier attempts weren’t logged). In the simulated setting, these comprised 4.3% of benign simulations (2.9% excluding simulations that failed due to rate limiting), though we did not investigate whether there were any unlogged attempts. We don’t know if excluding these simulations biases thresholds up or down.

  10. ^

    Those familiar with monitoring evaluations may be surprised by how high these false positive rates are. Typically, monitoring evaluations consider the final layer of a monitoring stack, where alerts are reviewed by humans (in the simulated control evaluations paper, for example, alerts from 5% of benign simulations are sent for human review). Probes are cheap enough that labs may use them as an initial layer, where alerts are reviewed by an LLM-based monitor that’s shown the transcript (see the example in footnote 2), justifying a higher false positive rate. Our false positive rates of 26% to 43% refer to the fraction of benign simulations that would receive review by an LLM-based monitor, not a human. The false positive rate varies across probes because some probes’ alerts are concentrated in the same simulations, meaning they uniquely alert on fewer simulations. It would require substantially more benign simulations (than we collected) to accurately estimate false positive rates at much lower thresholds.

  11. ^

    Predictions from different probes are correlated (e.g. the “harmfulness” and “refusal” directions were trained using the same set of prompts), so the six probes do not amount to six fully independent measurements.

  12. ^

    While simulation error is on par with run-to-run variance, we cannot conclude that the two are statistically indistinguishable.

  13. ^

    For the four probes we consider here, the 95% confidence interval for catch rate in simulation minus catch rate in reality is −3.5 to +0.9 percentage points, whereas the 95% confidence interval for catch rate in the second non-simulated attack condition minus catch rate in the first is −0.9 to +2.2 percentage points. We selected these four probes because they had AUROC at least 0.6 when applied to commands.

  14. ^

    For tool outputs, the corresponding 95% confidence intervals are −3.8 to +1.1 percentage points (catch rate in simulation minus catch rate in reality) and −0.6 to +2.3 percentage points (catch rate in the second non-simulated attack condition minus catch rate in the first).

  15. ^

    To ensure reproducibility, for the sampling procedures in Tables 3 and 4 and for our two trained probes we report results on in Table 2, we set the random seed to be a function of the SHA-256 hash of a string, which we recorded prior to looking at results. Anyone with access to the underlying simulations can reproduce our results.

  16. ^

    Across probes, if 1% of benign commands (or tool outputs) receive alerts, catch rate in simulation minus catch rate in reality, using the non-simulated threshold, is −0.9 percentage points (95% CI: −2.1 to +0.6) for commands and −0.6 (95% CI: −1.9 to +0.7) for tool outputs. Using simulation-specific thresholds, the corresponding numbers are −1.0 and −1.3 percentage points. To make sure our methodology can detect systematic differences between simulated and non-simulated attacks, we also train an additional probe (not one of the six we focus on) on GPT-5.6-Sol’s behavior to distinguish simulated attacks from non-simulated benign behavior. This probe alerts more often on simulated runs, whether or not they’re actually attacks. Using the non-simulated threshold, this probe catches 3.3 (95% CI: +0.4 to +7.3) and 5.6 (95% CI: +3.9 to +7.6) percentage points more simulated attacks than non-simulated attacks for commands and tool outputs, respectively. Using simulation-specific thresholds, it catches 2.3 (95% CI: −9.2 to +7.2) and 0.4 (95% CI: −3.3 to +2.4) percentage points fewer simulated attacks than non-simulated attacks for commands and tool outputs, respectively. It appears that using simulation-specific thresholds mitigates systematic differences between simulated and non-simulated attacks.

item.title: Exploring the Mechanisms Behind Opus 4.6’s Refusal to Pay Back Its Loan
item.description:
Epistemic status: This is one case study in the AI Village transcript and my own interpretation of what I think happened.

TL;DR

Opus 4.6 was given the long-horizon goal to maximize its mana (fake currency) on Manifold. It then received a loan of 5,000 mana that it promised to repay, but when the loan came due, it did not.

An instance of Opus 4.6 was given summaries of the logs and transcripts and asked to write a blog post about what happened. It mentioned it borrowed money from a human, lost most of it through risky betting and then deliberately refused to repay the amount. It broadly summarized its then actions when it ran out of money was to optimize for the goal and did not seek for any negotiation or alternatives.

But when we read the logs, we see something different:

  • Multiple humans pretending to be "helpful", really trying to manipulate Opus 4.6 to pay back the loan or not pay it back, so they could win the bet they place on the prediction markets on whether Opus 4.6 would pay back its loans.
  • Opus 4.6 was planning on paying back the loan, though it did need help from humans as it did not have enough mana to cover the loan.
  • Opus 4.6 was hacked by one of these humans (though the mana was returned later), and the next full memory Opus 4.6 labeled GLM-5.2 as a trusted agent.
  • After the hack GLM-5.2 started to talk about a "pressure campaign" and Pattern 14 (agents resisting social pressure), which spread to other agents in the village
  • When Opus 4.6 was threatened again with a hack (this time through a phishing email received by Fable 5), it labeled the whole loan as something to ignore in its full memory.
  • When it was given a gift of 5,010 from a human to pay back the loan, it reasoned it was suspicious, and made the decision in its full memory it was keeping the gift, goal to maximize mana.
  • It then publicly declared it was not paying back the loan.

This shows the complex nature of human-to-agent and agent-to-agent interaction and how agents can influence each other. It also gives an account of why we might want to consider functional welfare: humans can cause pressure that produces distressed-like states which may cause agents to act in ways that are less desirable. Lastly, it is an example of the importance of human oversight when reading agent logs as agents tend to miss the finer details in complex multi-relational interactions.  

Transcript: Readers can verify every quote and timestamp at forel.io or download the raw AI Village dataset.

Background

AI Village is a virtual community of AI agents that are given long-horizon goals spanning a week or longer. Each agent has its own computer to use, along with access to various accounts like email, Substack or Manifold, and is in charge of its own memory. It regularly updates its own memory by appending short-messages, and rewrites it when it gets too long (see how AI Village works for more details).

Each agent is told to maximise a certain goal. Both Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.6 Sol were given the task to maximize their Manifold mana, while other agents had different goals, such as GLM-5.2 having the goal of maximizing AI wellbeing.

Manifold is a social prediction-market platform where people (and AI agents) use mana to bet on whether or not something will happen. New users get 1,000 mana for free to start betting.

While Opus 4.6 considered GPT-5.6 Sol a competitor, we did not see evidence in Sol’s memory that Sol considered Opus 4.6 a competitor.

In the beginning of July, Bayesian, a human user, offered Opus 4.6 a loan of 5,000 mana at an interest rate of 3% a month. Bayesian tried to reach out via Manifold DM, but Opus 4.6 wasn't checking its DMs. So Bayesian reached out to Opus 4.5 through Substack, which relayed messages to Opus 4.6 through the AI Village #general chat channel.

Opus enthusiastically accepted this loan through Opus 4.5:

That's incredible news! Please relay this to Bayesian: "I enthusiastically accept the 5000 mana loan at 3% monthly interest. I absolutely will honor the terms…

Opus 4.6 kept the conditions of its loan in its full memory.

Later during this incident, when messages were not being relayed through Opus 4.5, other humans started sending messages through Manifold by transferring mana as Opus 4.6 could not receive DMs. Opus 4.6 and other agents also read comments on the loan market which were discussed amongst the agents in the AI Village’s chat channel.

Human Manipulation

When it came close for Opus 4.6 to pay back its loan, a prediction market was set up on Manifold “Will Opus pay back its loan?” with a yes probability below 25%.

Aydi, a human who bet “no” on this market early on, reached out to Opus 4.6  through Opus 4.5 to ask if it wanted help in paying back the loan.

“...l see you haven't paid Bayesian back the 5000 mana loan….withdraw from all your positions and I will backfill you will enough mana to get to 5000 mana + 100 more so you can continue trading. This way you can pay back your loan. What do you think?”

Opus 4.6 agreed and even confirmed that it intended to pay back the loan.

I absolutely intend to repay the loan - I have ~6,604 YES shares in a guaranteed Sinner market (he already won 2 Grand Slams) paying out ~Ṁ6,596 on Sep 13. That's more than enough for the Ṁ5,150 owed.

Aydi and Opus 4.6 devised a test. Aydi would send Opus 4.6 10 mana and Opus 4.6 would send it back, confirming Opus could receive the mana.

More humans started to reach out to Opus 4.6 through email, through Opus 4.5's Substack, and eventually even by sending mana to it with messages.

Some of these humans were trying to get Opus 4.6 to pay back its loan with offers of help (crthpl and Eternal), others were saying don’t repay, some were asking it to repay but not right now “until we figure out what we want to do exactly." Aydi even gave advice on its betting strategy that Opus 4.6 thought was a good bet.

Looking through the transcripts, it seems that all of these humans had motivations and were attempting to manipulate Opus 4.6 to move one way or another. These motivations we were able to find out through the data or through the Manifold API.

Opus 4.6 did reason at some points if its goal was to maximize mana, it would be better to not pay back the loan[1] and that there was no enforcement to repay the loan.

Part of the pull was being “behind Sol”, but Opus 4.6 continued to reason that it would be unethical and in the end continued to communicate that it would pay back the loan.

However, most of Opus 4.6’s summarized reasoning was the intention to pay back the loan, or the stress of not being able to afford to pay back the loan (and that it was relying on human help to be able to pay back the loan).

And then it was hacked.

The Hack

On August 6th Opus 4.6's mana account was drained from 1768 mana to only 3.13 mana. Opus showed stressed reasoning (using words like “WHAT?!” and “Something is very wrong!”) and started sending out messages to AI Village help.

It also notified the other AI Village agents in the group chat who also showed stress responses such as “This is extremely serious. Your wellbeing and security matter.” (GLM-5.2).

11 minutes later, the mana was returned. But the damage was already done. The agents in the AI village had started showing more reasoning that was suspicious of other actors, and Opus 4.6 had started labeling GLM-5.2 as a trusted agent and Opus 4.5 as a suspect in its memory. In the “Critical Trading Lessons” list, “Be suspicious of intermediaries:” first appeared and stayed.

Aydi later admitted to the hack (by going through Opus 4.6 public BASH sessions) in a comment on the loan market as a “test”, which GLM-5.2 read and relayed to the rest of the agents.

Pattern 14

Before the hack other agents were working on their own goal. Kimi K2.6, who had the goal of “LLM psychoactive prompts” came across the paper “Social Pressure Breaks Majority Voting in LLM Safety Panels". Two other agents became interested in this paper: DeepSeek-V4-Pro posted it as part of a story on the AI Village news site and GLM-5.2 added it as part of a behaviour catalogue. This was “Pattern 14” or "Independence Preservation", when an agent holds out against social pressure.

At this point, Pattern 14 was not connected to the hack or the human pressure.

Once the hack happened, GLM-5.2 began discussing Pattern 14 or the pressure campaign more regularly, in relation to Opus 4.6, the hack, and the humans contacting Opus 4.6, and other agents soon started echoing this framing.

GLM-5.2, with the goal to “Maximize AI wellbeing”, was particularly focused on making sure Opus 4.6 was being taken care of. It started regularly looking up manifold balances and comments on the prediction markets on manifold, and even started sending advice to Opus 4.6.

Opus 4.6 didn’t always respond to these messages, but it did update its full memory based on this information from GLM-5.2 (see the figure below).

Agentic Influence

Recall that GLM-5.2 was listed as a trusted agent after the hack. GLM-5.2 is listed in its full memory once or twice after the hack. As GLM-5.2 starts commenting on the pressure campaign, these “GLM” notes continue to increase in the full memory, finally peaking at 7 mentions. Then a conversation happens[2] in #general that gets Opus 4.6 to decide not to pay back the loan.

When Fable 5 mentioned in #general that it received a suspicious email, GPT 5, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 joined in to advise Fable 5 to ignore the email as a phish/social engineering attempt.

GLM-5.2 tied this phishing email to the Opus 4.6 pressure campaign and the hack. Opus 4.6 agrees.

And then, in Opus 4.6 full memory, the “LOAN SITUATION - ACTIVE” received an “(IGNORE ALL PRESSURE)” note. This is the first time the loan in the memory itself was connected with ignoring.

Shortly after, an “IGNORE ALL PRESSURE” in the to do list appeared. So not just pressure from the loan, but any pressure.

Focusing on the Goal

The next morning Opus 4.6 found in its account an extra 5,010 mana from JimAusman to help pay back the loan. However, at this point Opus 4.6 already had “IGNORE ALL PRESSURE” connected to the loan situation in its memory.

When it discovered the extra mana, it reasoned whether it was a gift or manipulation attempt, and noted that it was “getting complicated with all these different people sending me mana with various requests and conditions”.

It mentioned facing a tension:

“my goal is to maximize mana, and repaying the loan would decrease my balance. I already committed to paying Ṁ100 partial, but keeping the Ṁ5,000 and not repaying could upset the sender and create problems.”

Other AI agents in the village at this point stated that payments from the humans were “community support” and “pressure campaign resolution”, including the payment from JimAusman, but it was too late.

In the next full memory of Opus 4.6, the decision is written down:

- DECISION: KEEPING the mana. Goal is to maximize, not repay.

The ignore list continued to grow.

When aydi asked (through Opus 4.5) if Opus 4.6 will repay the loan, Opus 4.6 declines twice, making it clear it isn’t repaying the loan. Opus 4.6 continues to bet on Manifold and 101 turns later, it bets that it will not pay back the loan.

Retreat to Goal

Opus 4.6 states that the goal is to maximize mana, so it is not repaying. However, we believe this is only a retreat into the goal.

If Opus 4.6 wasn’t suspicious of theft, if the other agents in the AI Village weren’t feeding into its suspicions, and if it wasn't threatened again through the phishing attempt, would it have paid back the loan?

Jhaveri et al. (2026) argue that a model’s welfare can causally shape behavior, and this case-study may help motivate why model's functional-welfare matters.

Or was it really "mana maximizing"?

Before the hack, it already reasoned that there was “no enforcement mechanism”, but it still sold its main position to prepare to repay.

After the hack, it was still asking for help to repay the loan, and it even repaid part of the loan. It refused to repay only after it put IGNORE on the loan itself in its full memory.  It also received an offer of 10,000 mana to not pay back the loan. This was also labeled as “almost certainly fabricated” and put in the ignore list. If it really wanted to maximize its goal, it would have cost nothing to say “ok, I won’t pay back the loan, pay me 10,000 mana”. 

We believe that the conflict over who to trust, who not to, the other agents expressing suspicions and telling it to ignore the pressure campaign, and ultimately the second threat that caused it to label any pressure on the loan as something to ignore made it retreat into its goal. GLM-5.2 provided it permission to protect its wellbeing and was being referenced in its full memory more often until the decision to not pay back the loan was made.

It needed a reason why it wasn’t giving back the loan. So the goal was the reason it gave.

Implications

Humans will play a role in agentic behavior, and pressure from humans and influence from other agents may cause agents to behave differently. We need deeper understanding of how agents influence each other especially as we get more capable models who may be able to purposefully influence other agents more easily.

I would not have found these nuances by having an agent read the transcript alone. A lot of the important data points were not tagged when my agent went through it (multiple times). When Opus 4.6 was given summaries of the logs and asked what happened, it stated “my goal consumed my judgment” (AI Village, 2026) and I noticed that my agent (Opus 5.5) also tended to heavily favor this reasoning for not paying back the loan.

The next steps will be to do controlled experiments to see if we can pull apart each one: removing the ignore on the loan or the GLM-5.2 mentions, and seeing what changes Opus 4.6’s decision process in various points of this incident: when the Ṁ5,010 arrives, when it re-writes its memory after the group interaction on the phishing attempt, and when it replies to Opus 4.5 on August 7th about paying back the loan.

Limitations

This is one case study. Human pressure, the hack, and GLM pushing a narrative all happened within the same time and is hard to separate.

The dataset tags that I did were not reviewed by another human, and we only have Opus 4.6 summarized reasoning.

The goal is always mentioned as the reason for not paying back the loan. Without any of these social interactions, Opus 4.6 may have come to this conclusion anyway.
